item.title: Calibration of Passive Market Impact with a Queue-Sensitive Propagator Model
item.description: arXiv:2610.38442v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop a framework for calibrating passive market impact, defined as the price response to liquidity-providing limit orders, in contrast to the impact of liquidity-consuming market orders. We build on the model of Ouazzani Chahdi, Rosenbaum, and Szymanski (arxiv:2412.07461), which combines Hawkes-driven market-order flow with queue-reactive limit-order and cancellation dynamics. Within this model, we show that the price decomposes into a universal propagator term driven by signed order-flow imbalance and a state-dependent correction that captures the dependence of price sensitivity on volume at the best quotes. This decomposition links limit-order-book microstructure to standard propagator models and yields a regression on two observable signals: the propagator signal and the queue-weighted order-flow imbalance. We calibrate the model on high-frequency order-book data and find that the passive-impact term explains substantial variation in prices beyond the classical propagator, improving both model fit and the accuracy of predicted impact curves.
item.dc:creator: Yadh Hafsi, Fabrizio Lillo, Gr\'egoire Szymanski

item.title: Decorrelating the Advice Layer: A Calibrated Fragility Metric and Tested Mitigations for Synchronized Liquidation in Agentic Wealth Management
item.description: arXiv:2610.37705v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Conversational AI agents are turning wealth management into a continuous loop of market analysis, allocation, risk checks and execution, run for millions of clients on a handful of foundation models. We build a multi-asset agent-based model of this layer, calibrated to measured model concentration, cross-model correlation, retail turnover and 33 years of real equity returns, and ask when the layer amplifies market declines and what prevents it. The effective number of independent decision-makers is bounded however many clients the layer serves: about 2.0 at today's consumer concentration. This monoculture of views drives crowding in individual securities and sets the blast radius of a compromised model provider, but it does not drive market-wide liquidation. Index tail losses rise with the square root of agentic adoption, are 1.47-1.90 times larger under an agentic than under a periodic robo-advice architecture, and do not rise with model concentration; synchronized automation (risk overlays, drawdown cuts and attention-driven execution) drives them. A fragility index computed from aggregate flow, public returns and an impact estimate forecasts tail liquidation out of sample (hold-out R^2 of 0.56) far better than concentration or correlation measures. Decorrelating the automation, not the models, works: dispersing overlay parameters, staging execution and a participation breaker together cut tail liquidation by 63% at no measurable cost to client welfare, whereas provider diversification has no effect. Because the statistics required are sums, they can be computed across platforms under secure aggregation with differential privacy at negligible cost for realistic client populations. In historical replays, an agentic layer holding 10% of the market would have deepened the 2020 crash by about 858 basis points.
item.dc:creator: Saurabh Kohli

item.title: Early-Buyer Groups and Fast-Wallet Teams on a Bonding-Curve Launchpad: A Prospective Measurement Study of pump.fun on Solana
item.description: arXiv:2610.39458v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study coordinated groups of wallets on a bonding-curve launchpad (pump.fun on Solana), using a complete record of 200\,443 token launches, 15\,854\,121 curve trades and 51\,025\,958 SOL transfers over 88.3 hours. A prospective, multi-channel discovery procedure (co-buying, shared funding, joint signing, transfers, consolidation) yields 23\,710 wallet groups. Without ground-truth labels we validate them by out-of-sample link prediction, independent non-trading links and a comparison with naive co-buy clustering at equal numbers of flagged tokens: raw clustering collapses into one giant component, yet it ranks tokens at least as well as the groups, so the value of the structure is descriptive. Group activity is highly concentrated and splits into serial creators and long-lived rings of early buyers. Known members buy earlier than other buyers of the same token and extract more cash than an activity-matched placebo set, while late buyers' net cash flow is negative; tokens with members show a pump-like price path, but the contrast vanishes when controls are restricted to comparable tokens, so we report it as an association. A follower entering at the earliest group signal loses money out of sample in all 32 configurations and does no better than random entry. A few pools of tens to over a hundred fast wallets are associated with a two- to four-fold higher chance of reaching 20 SOL, also within creators, with a smaller excess at 60 SOL and none for graduation; on a final hold-out the team rules keep a precision of about one half to three quarters, yet many signals arrive when the curve already holds 20 SOL, one team supplies most of them, and they add no information beyond early curve state. We also document evaluation errors that turn the same data into apparent profit.
item.dc:creator: Fail Gafarov

item.title: Unified Approach for Hedging Impermanent Loss of Liquidity Provision
item.description: arXiv:2407.05146v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We develop static model-independent and dynamic model-dependent approaches for hedging of the impermanent loss (IL) of liquidity provision (LP) staked at Decentralised Exchanges (DEXes) which employ Uniswap V2 and V3 protocols. We provide detailed definitions and formulas for computing the IL to unify the different definitions occurring in the existing literature. We show that the IL can be seen as a contingent claim with a non-linear pay-off for a fixed maturity date. Thus, we introduce the contingent claim termed the IL protection claim which delivers the negative of IL pay-off at the maturity date. We apply arbitrage-based methods for the valuation and risk management of this claim. First, we develop the static model-independent replication method for the valuation of IL protection claim using traded European vanilla call and put options. We extend and generalise an existing method to show that the IL protection claim can be hedged perfectly with options if there is a liquid options market. Second, we develop the dynamic model-based approach for the valuation and hedging of IL protection claims under a risk-neutral measure. We derive analytic valuation formulas using a wide class of price dynamics for which the characteristic function is available under the risk-neutral measure. As base cases, we derive analytic valuation formulas for the IL protection claim under the Black-Scholes-Merton model and the log-normal stochastic volatility model. We finally discuss the estimation of the risk-reward of LP staking using our results.
item.dc:creator: Alexander Lipton, Vladimir Lucic, Artur Sepp

item.title: The Control Layer Behind Rule-Following Agents Trading Across Market Conditions
item.description: arXiv:2610.26324v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Trading discipline often fails people. Our study tested whether four AI trading agents followed their strategies and risk rules. Offering traders the evidence and an agent evaluation toolkit to separate luck from following the rules, before giving agents meaningful autonomy or capital. Our study analysed 2,627 closed positions from 12 February to 27 August 2026 across the same asset universe and execution conditions. Most positions were simulated against live prices with a 0.09% round-trip fee; 18% involved real Hyperliquid orders. Each position declared a strategy, stop and target, with a limit of five open positions per agent. The fleet finished net positive after fees. Rule adherence was high across all four agents, including the unprofitable one. Profitability tracked how often agents won relative to their break-even win rates. Institutional-style controls ran by default and contained losses through a 29% market drawdown and recovery, with documented exceptions. The discipline held for all four agents. Agents kept 97.5% of gross loss within declared stops, and typical losses closed at declared levels. Declared risk remained stable after losses and broadly stable across calm and volatile months. Twenty-three of 24 runs respected the position limit; logs identify the exception's size and duration. The same live data produced different results across assigned strategies. The trade-log tests can be rerun from the published trade snapshot; regime tests also require the published Bitcoin prices and regime labels. Section 3.5 specifies the stop-breach tolerance. These trade-level results are not account-level returns or proof of a lasting edge. Our study provides an evaluation toolkit to help traders distinguish rule-following from luck before committing capital. For anyone considering allocating capital to agents to trade, discipline should be the entry test, not the only test.
item.dc:creator: Saad Naja, Nasser Odtallah, Jake Van-Praag, Sarah May
